title: The Teacher Who Cannot Tell
author: Becky Allen
summary: When a teacher revises an AI-generated lesson plan, the edits carry meaning that neither the teacher nor any outside reviewer can fully decode—because teacher judgment blends factual corrections, learning science applications, pedagogical content knowledge, and personal aesthetic preference in ways that feel identical from inside the teacher's own experience. Becky Allen traces four distinct categories of what she calls "teacher taste": compressed knowledge about learners calibrated through years of watching students struggle; teacher-lesson fit, where an explanation works partly because of how a specific teacher inhabits it; values and commitments about what a subject is for; and plain preference or convention. The problem is that all four arrive as the same internal signal—a flash of "no, not like that"—making it impossible even for the teacher to know which type of judgment produced which edit. Research complicates consensus-based validation: Strong, Gargani, and Hacifazlioglu found that experienced observers who agreed with each other largely failed to identify which teachers' students actually learned more, suggesting professional consensus may reflect shared training and convention as much as signal about learning. The epistemically uncomfortable conclusion is that each teacher revision is a conjecture about where learning might fail—not a verdict—and only real learners in real classrooms can test whether any version of a lesson is better than another.
points: Teacher edits to AI-generated lessons blend at least four distinct categories—factual corrections, learning science judgments, pedagogical content knowledge, and preference—but from inside the teacher's experience, all four arrive as the same intuitive signal, making it impossible to know which edits will actually improve student learning.

Some 'teacher taste' is compressed knowledge calibrated through years of watching learners: the teacher doesn't retrieve a principle, she senses a lesson won't work—and this sense may be genuinely predictive of student struggle even when it cannot be articulated.

Teacher-lesson fit means some edits improve student outcomes only when that specific teacher delivers the lesson; the revised version isn't generically superior, it's better for this teacher in this room—a fact that limits what teacher review can validate.

Agreement among teachers about lesson quality is narrower evidence than it appears: shared professional training means errors are unlikely to be independent, and research found that experienced observers' holistic judgments of teacher quality failed to predict which teachers' students actually achieved more.

Teacher review of AI-generated lessons is not futile but must be understood as conjecture rather than verdict: each edit proposes a hypothesis about where learning may fail, and that hypothesis can only be tested against real learners—not simulated by AI or validated by peer consensus.
quotes: When a teacher changes a lesson, what kind of signal have we received? And how would anyone, including the teacher, know when their revision will improve student learning?

But knowing the principles does not settle how they should be applied. As I argued in Lessons Worth Arguing About, good principles collide. The concrete example that makes an idea immediately comprehensible may obscure the more general structure.

The teacher may not experience herself as retrieving knowledge at all. She just reads the lesson and senses that it will not work. That sense can arise in several ways. She may recognise the shape of a lesson that has failed before. She may recall a specific pupil or teaching episode.

these forms of taste do not necessarily feel different from the inside. A calibrated prediction about novice confusion, a lesson that better fits the teacher’s performance, a commitment about the purpose of the subject and a familiar aesthetic all arrive with the same little flash of “no, not like that”. The teacher experiences each edit as the lesson becoming better.

Strong, Gargani and Hacifazlioglu demonstrated the distinction uncomfortably. Experienced educators watched teachers whose value-added effectiveness was already known. The judges agreed reasonably well with one another, but largely failed to identify the teachers whose pupils made greater achievement gains.

Agreement is evidence, but evidence of a narrower kind than we want. It tells us that the preference is shared and reproducible. That may be because teachers have independently learned the same regularity about pupils. But teachers may also agree because they received similar training, inherited the same conventions, hold the same beliefs about good teaching or possess the same professional blind spots. Their errors are unlikely to be independent.

the model cannot verify a lesson by pretending to be a student, and the teacher cannot verify it by declaring she prefers one version. Both can show us where to look. Only learners can tell us what the lesson taught.
